title: How Elimination Diets Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain elimination diets: a medical procedure (originally run by doctors or nutritionists) in which a person removes suspect foods from their diet, then reintroduces them one food group at a time to identify triggers for symptoms like IBS, headaches, fatigue or mood problems. They distinguish food allergies (immune-system mistaken identity, dangerous even in tiny amounts), gluten intolerance and celiac disease, and food sensitivities (poorly understood, dose-dependent), and discuss the FODMAPs idea from Australian doctor Peter Gibson. They walk through the four phases (planning and food journaling, elimination, challenge/reintroduction, and evaluation) using a hypothetical couple, Brenda and Eddie. They warn about pitfalls such as nutrient deficiency, orthorexia (obsession with clean or healthy eating, described through Hannah Matthews's article), and DIY diets promoted by non-experts. The episode ends with a sponsorship pitch for the Thousand Girls Initiative from COED in Guatemala.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to elimination diets
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the name 'elimination' and mistakenly link it to pooping out food. Chuck introduces elimination diets as a trendy practice of removing foods and adding them back to find triggers for symptoms, and notes they are often done on one's own rather than with a professional.

segments.title: Medical origins, skin prick and blood tests
segments.summary: Elimination diets began as a medical procedure prescribed by doctors or nutritionists for patients with unexplained symptoms. The hosts note that skin prick tests and blood tests for food allergies and sensitivities are unreliable, with blood tests giving false positives often, and that many Americans think they have a food allergy when few do.

segments.title: Allergies as mistaken immune identity
segments.summary: Food allergies are explained as the immune system mistakenly treating a harmless food like a strawberry as a pathogen. Even tiny amounts can trigger a reaction, and allergies can be life threatening.

segments.title: Intolerances, celiac disease, and sensitivities
segments.summary: Intolerance is a digestive system response, often from a missing enzyme, and can cause cramps, bloating and mood effects tied to the gut-brain connection. Celiac disease has an immune component, unlike gluten intolerance. Sensitivities are poorly understood, and dose matters: small amounts may be tolerated while large amounts cause symptoms. The hosts also mention MSG and the 'Chinese food syndrome' stigma.

segments.title: Peter Gibson and FODMAPs
segments.summary: Australian doctor Peter Gibson proved non-celiac gluten sensitivity was real in 2011 but later found placebo groups had similar symptoms. He has since pointed to FODMAPs, a type of carbohydrate found in gluten and wheat as well as other foods, as a likely culprit.

segments.title: Four phases of an elimination diet: planning and elimination
segments.summary: Using hypothetical couple Brenda and Eddie, the hosts describe planning, including listing symptoms, suspect foods, and keeping a food journal, and noting cravings can signal culprits. They then describe the elimination phase, cutting out suspect food groups such as dairy and sugar for two to three weeks, and the need to supplement nutrients like calcium or vitamin D.

segments.title: Challenge phase and reintroducing foods
segments.summary: In the challenge phase, foods are reintroduced one at a time and symptoms watched for, for example dairy for a day followed by two days back on the elimination diet. Foods that do not cause symptoms stay in the diet, and the hosts note that mixing foods during challenges and broad food groups make results confusing. They also distinguish dose-dependent sensitivities from allergies.

segments.title: Pitfalls: cross-reactive foods, orthorexia and DIY advice
segments.summary: The hosts discuss cross-reactive foods, such as latex allergy linked to certain fruits, and risks of nutrient deficiency. They discuss orthorexia, an obsession with clean or healthy eating, through Hannah Matthews's article about her slide into anorexia. They criticize unqualified self-proclaimed experts promoting DIY elimination diets and urge consulting a professional.

segments.title: Closing reflections on food and healthy middle ground
segments.summary: Chuck reflects on his changing attitude toward food after reading about orthorexia, noting that obsessing over healthy versus toxic food can signal a deeper relationship issue. The hosts conclude that a healthy middle ground is needed.

segments.title: COED Thousand Girls Initiative sponsorship
segments.summary: A sponsor plug for COED and its Thousand Girls Initiative in Guatemala, which keeps girls in school through a book fund and sponsorship at forty or eighty dollars a month.
